opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's because this is the period where the work stops being a set of benchmark results and starts being molecules that matter to someone's actual program.

For the last few years, a lot of the conversation in AI for drug discovery has been about retrospective performance. How well do you predict structures you've already seen, how do you do on a held-out test set. That's important, and we've put a lot of effort into it, but it's not the thing a medicinal chemist or a biologist at a pharma company ultimately cares about. They care about whether this helps them get to a better molecule faster, on a target they're actually working on, where the answer isn't already in the literature.

What's exciting about the next six to twelve months is that we get that feedback loop for real. When you put models into the hands of teams working on live programs, you learn things you'd never learn internally. You find out where the model is surprisingly useful, where it's overconfident, and what kinds of design problems people bring to it that you didn't anticipate. Each of those becomes signal for making the next version better.

There's also a shift in what we're asking the models to do. Prediction is one thing: given this protein and this molecule, what does the complex look like? Design is harder and more valuable: given this target, propose something that binds the way you want, with properties you can actually develop. Seeing how well that holds up when partners take designs into the wet lab, at scale and across diverse targets, is the real test. If the hit rates and the quality of what comes out look like what we've been seeing internally, that changes the economics of early discovery quite a bit.

And I think it matters for the field more broadly. There's healthy skepticism in pharma about AI, partly earned, because there's been a lot of hype. The way you get past that isn't by making bigger claims. It's by working closely with people who have high standards and letting the results speak. So for me, this next stretch is about learning fast, being honest about what works and what doesn't, and hopefully showing that these tools can change how quickly we go from a biological idea to a real therapeutic candidate.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, what I'm most excited about is that this is the moment where the models stop being a demo and start touching real programs. For the last few years, the story in AI for biology has been benchmarks. You release a model, you show it does well on a structure prediction task or a binder design task, people get excited, and then there's this long gap before anyone's medicine is actually different because of it. The deployments we're doing now with pharma partners are about closing that gap.

Concretely, what that looks like is we take a target the partner actually cares about, often one they've struggled with, sometimes for years, and we go from a sequence or a structure to designed molecules, antibodies especially, that get made and tested in their labs. And the thing that gets me up in the morning is that the loop is tight. We're not waiting eighteen months to find out if the idea was good. We're seeing wet lab results come back in weeks, and that data feeds right back into how we think about the models.

The other reason I'm excited is that these partners are stress testing us in ways we can't do ourselves. Internally you can convince yourself a model is great. A pharma team with twenty years of experience on a target class will immediately tell you where it falls down. Where does it struggle with developability? Where are the designs too similar to each other? Where does the model confidently predict something that just doesn't express? That feedback is gold. It's the difference between building something that looks good on a leaderboard and building something a medicinal chemist or an antibody engineer actually wants to use every day.

And then the last piece is just what it unlocks scientifically. If you can reliably generate functional binders against hard targets, the question shifts from "can we make a molecule" to "which molecule should we make." That's a completely different conversation to be having with a pharma partner. You start talking about targets they'd written off, about going after multiple epitopes at once, about designing the whole molecule rather than just optimizing a hit. Over the next six to twelve months I think we'll have a handful of those stories where the answer was genuinely enabled by the model, and that's the kind of evidence that changes how the whole industry thinks about this.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is getting to see how these models perform on problems that matter to drug discovery. Designing a molecule computationally is one step; testing it and learning whether it has the properties you need is where the real feedback comes from.

Over the next six to twelve months, the opportunity with pharmaceutical partners is to bring those pieces together: work on a relevant problem, make predictions, test the molecules, and use those results to improve the next round. I’m excited to learn where that process can help teams move faster and where we still need to improve. Ultimately, the question is whether we can help them make better molecules and pursue ideas that would otherwise be difficult to explore.

What excites me is the opportunity to see how these models perform on the problems that pharmaceutical teams actually care about. Designing a molecule computationally is one step; making it, testing it, and learning whether it has the properties you need is where the real feedback comes from.

Over the next six to twelve months, I’m excited to learn where we can make that cycle faster and more productive. Can we help teams explore ideas they wouldn’t otherwise test? Can we get them to promising candidates with fewer rounds of experimentation? Those are the kinds of outcomes that would make these deployments meaningful.
